author: qlte
story: Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data
parent:
This is very, very weak.

Clinical science is inundated with well-reasoned "potential leads". Ideas for targets, and even designing drugs to interact with those targets in the desired way, is not the bottleneck. Hasn't been for decades. The bottleneck is in clinical development i.e. human trials.

There are many many AI drug discovery companies out there, many of them very well funded, and ALL of them with no shortage of "potential leads".

These companies usually start out with the idea that their potential leads are better than the alternatives (generally because they cast a much bigger net/ considered more screening criteria than a human could, thanks to AI) and that big pharma will pay them license fees.

And yet, all of those companies, pretty much without exception, have turned into drug development companies themselves. They are forced to develop their own "potential leads" into actual approved drugs. And they are subject to the same timelines, same costs and - so far - the same probabilities of success as any other drug developer.

PerturbAI & OpenAI's "potential leads" might be better or worse than the next AI company. I would guess worse, given there is zero proprietary data involved and no clarity about why the underlying models are going to generate insightful findings. Either way, not useful.
text:
I just saw a similar post from Anthropic which also landed like a thud. The deep need of OpenAI/Anthropic to churn out flashy announcements today to with upcoming IPO is in serious conflict with the realistic pace of biological or medical research, let alone successful clinical applications. They would produce many cool leads like this which ultimately turn out to be useless before landing on the one that makes it to human clinical trials (and may fail there too).

A previous blog post from Anthropic used the mention of "CRISPR-like" to activate a mini hype cycle by association with a well-known groundbreaking discovery. Without that kind of manipulative hook these announcements are pretty thin gruel and below the bar of thousands of Pubmed papers that never made it into public view.

author: kunai
story: Award-Winning AI Literature
parent:
The post is about ai literature winning awards. Since an award is supposed to be a measure of quality, not unit-cost, a trend of ai winning awards is either indicative of the quality of the writing or of a systemic flaw in how these awards are judged (which seems plausible too).

A van gogh painting is more valuable than a replica because 1. it is scarce and 2. owning one conveys prestige. A perfect replica of a van gogh painting conveys the same artistic expression as the original.
text:
> a trend of ai winning awards is either indicative of the quality of the writing or of a systemic flaw in how these awards are judged (which seems plausible too).

I definitely think this is plausible, and I think we need to start extending the idea of code "smells" to regular languages as well. I have TAed for literature and have reviewed many a manuscript and except for really really finely honed projects with lots of editing in post, written text almost always has many of these obvious smells (cliches, fallacies, illogical juxtapositions, poor cause and effect). AI-generated prose is no exception. Character names, phrases, descriptions of sensory experiences that are off or not quite right, improper negation (LLMs still struggles with the idea of 'scope'), sentence structure being very predictable and one-dimensional (even when using the latest models and mimicking famous authors and poets and even with very careful prompting), so on and so forth, you get the idea.

> A perfect replica of a van gogh painting conveys the same artistic expression as the original.

I think OP's example was a poor one. A perfect replica of a van gogh painting indeed does convey the same artistic expression as the original. However, I think the better comparison is an understudy's mimickry of A Starry Night which seems inspired by it and yet adds nothing to the original and is somewhat deficient in some ways, and misunderstands the artistic intent of the original. That would certainly not convey the same expression as the original, and would be met with widespread criticism.

author: islewis
story: Show HN: Hurston-1 open source TTS that speak Southern American and Afro-English
parent:
Hey HN, I’m open sourcing my Hurston-1 narrowband TTS model (Apache-2.0). It is very good with American English and does especially well with Southern American and Regional African English accents. Destined AI is based in Atlanta, and I built this because I’m amazed by what AI can do, and I wanted to help introduce and welcome more people to feel comfortable using and interacting with AI.

Since 2021, I’ve been collecting fully consented voice data from over 20,000 people, 1M audio recordings, and over 1,800 hrs of audio captured to date. For this model, I used a small part of the data, 136 hrs, to finetune Maya1 and expand it’s capabilities.

Hurston-1 is a narrowband TTS model that focuses the output on telephone use because that is still where most of these voices will be heard. I’ve used it to support customers such as Amazon and Salesforce and generated over half-mill revenue with it. Now I’m open sourcing it to help unlock opportunities for others as well.

Limitations: this model doesn’t maintain the exact same voice across prompts and doesn’t support voice cloning. For many use cases, this is fine but maybe not so - if you’re creating podcasts.

This is the first release - I’m already working on the next version with improvements.

I would appreciate, if anyone is interested in this space, download the model from huggingface, check it out and let me know any feedback. Also, open to connecting with others in this space as well.

Distilling just works too well. It costs much more to aggregate the data in the first place and train the first model, but once that exists and you are selling access, the second guy can train their model by using the first model to generate the training data.

The only ways to fight this is trying to either: 1. Block it by cutting off access, which is pretty tough because it basically means you cannot offer unmonitored access which is a no-no to a lot of customers, and even then the workload looks very similar to actual real workloads and if the company doing the distilling is a bit sneaky and using intermediaries etc it's almost impossible to stop, or:

2. Try to use IP law to block the practice, which is pretty gross given how they got the data in the first place, and so far no court has supported them on this. And even if they can make it illegal, it won't actually help because there are countries that see having top-tier AI as a national priority and will actually support their companies breaking laws to get there.

People misunderstand why Anthropic is being so stingy about granting access to their top models. It's not some kind of marketing ploy, they know that if they release them fully openly then there will be a Chinese open-weights model in 3 months that is just as good. Also the reason why they try to hide chain-of-thought and the probability distributions.

author: Twey
story: Sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust
parent:
> Sure, the same can be said of an async library

An generic future is much harder to be called like this. You need to to create wakers and if you don't properly handle them you'll busy loop. You also need to provide the exact runtime the future needs for its I/O.

> so long as you're okay with none of your other flows being able to make progress in the meantime

And isn't that what blocking code does all the time?

> ‘The best of both worlds’ means that it shares the advantages of both

If you look at it from the perspective of a caller:

- you can easily use it from blocking code without needing a runtime - you can easily use it from async code without blocking the executor

As such it does provide the best of both worlds to the caller.

It is true that it's the worst of both worlds for who is writing the Sans-IO library though.

> or, as we used to call it, pure functional programming

You can for sure describe this as "pure" and "functional", but I bet most people think of a different paradigm when talking about pure functional programming.
text:
> An generic future is much harder to be called like this. You need to to create wakers and if you don't properly handle them you'll busy loop. You also need to provide the exact runtime the future needs for its I/O.

You don't actually have to handle I/O with the async runtime if you don't want. You _could_ just poll the futures yourself in a loop, which is roughly the same as what happens if you just call the transition function in a loop for a manual state machine. And likewise if you just keep calling the transition function with empty input you'll also busy-loop.

> And isn't that what blocking code does all the time?

Sure, if you have only one flow you care about or you have threads to take care of your concurrency, this is fine. You can do it with any model (blocking, async, manual state machine).

> - you can easily use it from blocking code without needing a runtime - you can easily use it from async code without blocking the executor

But these things are already true of a state machine compiled from async/await instead of written by hand. `poll()` is just a function, and you can call it where you like. By the contract of `Future`, just like the contract of the state machine transition, it's guaranteed to ‘not block’. The waker machinery exists to help you write engines that decide when to poll, but if you've got your own external notion of that you're free to just call `poll()`. The standard library even has some optimization around this case, e.g. `Waker::noop()`.

> You can for sure describe this as "pure" and "functional", but I bet most people think of a different paradigm when talking about pure functional programming.

I agree, but it's confusing to me that this is the case. Original pure functional programming was all about ‘how can we write more useful programs without any effects’ and ‘what benefits can we get from doing so’. I think those questions are kind of answered; since Moggi's work in the early nineties it's been focused more on ‘how can we keep the benefits of pure functions while also being able to encode effectful logic?’, to which manually-written state machines are a rather primitive sort of answer. They bear pretty strong resemblance to iteratees/transducers/pipes/etc. from that lineage, except that those things aim to build a higher-level combinator language on top to reduce the amount of manual state-machine writing one has to do.

author: bigbadfeline
story: What Millions of Data Points Reveal About US Inflation
parent:
One shouldn't forget is that every dollar that's spent on something, is a dollar not spent on something else. As long as both options are domestic and does not involve money being sent abroad, increase in price of one product means decrease of price in another, so in a way, gas prices cannot move overall inflation at all: gas, becoming more expensive, made other things cheaper by suppressing demand on them.

In the old days, oil in the US was mostly imported, so that wasn't the case: higher oil price meant just less money left for anything else, so economy could fall while prices rose (stagflation). Now, this is no longer the case, higher oil prices mean more money for everyone because US is a net exporter.
text:
> gas, becoming more expensive, made other things cheaper by suppressing demand on them.

Nope, it may suppress demand for "other things" but doesn't make them cheaper. The making of "other things" uses gas too, as do their makers, so they have to increase their prices as well in order to compensate for the increased input costs.

The suppression of demand, if it materializes at all, has a natural floor, as does the reduction of margin - it's natural floor is 0 - past that, reduction of price is impossible. In fact, reduced output usually leads to higher costs per unit produced due to reduced economies of scale, as a result, lower demand often results in higher prices even if gas prices stay the same.

author: zaius
story: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
parent:
Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings.

Here's a quick demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BFfbXAwRq98

Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer.

As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman.

I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy.

To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp).

I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use.

Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

author: fsh
story: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
parent:
It's pretty obvious that Gemini 4 Carbon is not token efficient. It also has relatively low tokens-per-second compared to other models. I can think of several reasons why this is the case:

1. Google has huge amounts of cash and compute. Their goal was to train a model that that has the highest quality & frontier performance, not create a model that's efficient to run and serve. They have other models for that, like Hydrogen.

2. Google created Carbon without caring for inference costs. DeepMind is subsidized by the rest of Google's empire. Selling inference is an insignificant part of Google's revenue. But for Anthropic and OpenAI, selling inference is their entire business model. Anthropic and OpenAI have enormous incentive to sell as much inference as they can in the most efficient manner. Google doesn't have this incentive.

3. They are one of the few companies that can be inefficient. Out of all the frontier labs, Google DeepMind is probably the least constrained by compute. Chinese labs have around 10 to 100 times less compute, so they must release highly optimized models.
text: 4. Google did a worse job than Anthropic and OpenAI.
